q: Dark, heavy and so fine-grained that no crystals can be picked out, formed from lava that cooled in the open air, and weathering in time to a deep red earth. Which rock?
opts: Chalk
Basalt
Schist
Granite
exp: Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock on earth and floors most of its oceans. Because it cooled quickly its crystals are too small to see, which is the simplest way to tell it from granite, which cooled slowly underground and is full of crystals you can count.

q: Ash from an eruption settles metres deep, compacts and hardens into a rock soft enough to cut with a hand saw, and central Italian towns dug their cellars straight into it. What is that rock called?
opts: Basalt
Chalk
Tuff
Gneiss
exp: Tuff, tufo in Italian, is volcanic ash consolidated into rock rather than cooled lava, which is why it stays light and easily worked. A cellar cut into it holds a steady cool temperature all year with no machinery at all, and the same rock weathers into a light, porous vineyard soil.

q: Vines are planted one to a pit scooped through black volcanic grit, each pit ringed by a low crescent of dry stone against the wind, on an Atlantic island off the African coast. Where is this?
opts: Lanzarote
Madeira
Corsica
Sicily
exp: The black grit is lapilli thrown out by the eruptions of the 1730s, which buried a good part of the island's farmland metres deep. Each pit is scooped down through the grit to reach the older soil underneath, and the crescent of dry stone on the windward side keeps the Atlantic trade wind off the leaves. It is hand work from beginning to end, since no machine can farm a field of separate pits.

q: A merchant recommends a wine on the grounds that it grew on volcanic soil. Why does that description on its own tell you very little?
opts: Volcanic soils are so alike from place to place that the phrase adds nothing
It is a claim almost no vineyard anywhere in the world could honestly make
Volcanic rock breaks down far too slowly ever to have formed a soil at all
It names where the material came from, not whether it is clay, grit or bare rock
exp: Weathered basalt can make a dense red clay, fresh ash can be as loose as gravel, and a young flow may still be bare stone. Those three behave nothing alike in a dry August, so the useful question is what the material is like now rather than how it arrived.

q: A vineyard sits on a lava flow a few centuries old and its neighbour on ash that has been weathering for a hundred thousand years. Which has the deeper soil?
opts: The younger one, because a fresh flow is soft and crumbles readily
The younger one, because each eruption buries the older soil deeper
The older one, because turning rock into soil is very slow work
Neither, because ash and lava weather down at much the same rate
exp: Soil forms as water, frost, acid and roots break rock apart, and on hard volcanic rock that takes many thousands of years. It is why a young flow of solid lava carries almost nothing, while loose ash and lapilli need no such weathering and can hold a vine within a century or two of falling.

q: Stones in one vineyard are rounded and smooth, and in another sharp and angular. What made the difference?
opts: The rounded ones were tumbled along by water and the angular ones simply fell
The rounded ones were worn smooth by generations of ploughing the rows
The rounded ones are several million years older than the angular ones
The rounded ones are limestone and the angular ones are always granite
exp: A stone carried in a river bumps along the bed and loses its corners as it travels, quickly in a soft rock and only after many kilometres in a hard one, so roundness is a record of travel. Angular rubble at the foot of a cliff has not travelled at all, which lets you read something off the ground before anyone tells you the geology.

q: One Bordeaux district gave up describing itself and simply took the name of the ground it stands on. Which district?
opts: Graves
Sauternes
Pomerol
Margaux
exp: Graves is the French word for gravel. The beds of it were dropped by rivers running off the Pyrenees and the Massif Central during the ice ages, and the district was planted and famous long before the marshy ground to the north of it was drained.

q: Along a river valley the gravel lies in flat steps at several heights above the present water. Which of those steps is the oldest?
opts: The one furthest downstream, since a river carries its load seaward over time
The highest, laid down when the river ran at that level and left as it cut down
All of them equally, since a single flood laid the whole staircase at once
The lowest, since the material closest to the water has been there longest
exp: A river cuts downward over time and abandons its old bed as a terrace each time it drops. The highest terraces are therefore the oldest, and usually the stoniest and poorest, having had the longest for their fine material to wash out, which is why they are so often the ones planted.

q: A mountain stream comes out of its gorge onto the flat and spreads its load in a wide apron of stone and sand at the foot of the range. What is that landform called?
opts: An escarpment
A river terrace
A moraine
An alluvial fan
exp: Fans are among the most dependable vineyard ground in dry country: stony, free-draining and raised just enough above the valley floor for cold air to run off them. A fan is deep as well, since everything the mountains above have shed for thousands of years has come to rest on it, so roots can go a long way down before they meet rock.

q: A vineyard floor looks like nothing but stones, yet the vines on it have never gone short of water. What is holding it?
opts: The stones themselves, which are porous and act as a reservoir
The sand and clay packed between the stones, and often a clay layer beneath
Sea fog, which rolls in most mornings and wets the surface
Nothing at all, since such a vine survives on whatever rain falls that week
exp: Hard river stones shed rain and store heat but hold almost no water, so a vineyard floored with them lives on the fine material packed between and beneath them. It is why two gravel banks a hundred metres apart can behave completely differently, and why anyone assessing one digs down to see what lies under the stones.

q: Boulders sit at the head of a valley, gravel halfway down it and fine silt out on the plain beyond. What sorted them?
opts: Farmers, who carted the biggest stones up to the head of the valley over the centuries
The age of the rock, since the oldest beds always break into the largest pieces
The speed of the water, which drops the biggest material first as it slows
The wind, which rolls the coarse material up the valley and blows the fine out to the plain
exp: Moving water can carry a particle only up to a size set by how fast it is going, so a river unloads from the coarsest downward as it loses energy. That is why the gravel districts of the world sit where a river left the hills, and the clay ones further out where it finally slowed.

q: The morning after a summer downpour, the bottom row of a steep vineyard is buried in fine soil washed off the top of the slope. What is that process called?
opts: Chlorosis
Compaction
Erosion
Leaching
exp: A steep vineyard loses soil to every heavy rain, and on the classic slopes it has been carried back up by hand for centuries. Cover crops, walls and terraces all exist to slow the water down before it can pick the soil up and take it away.

q: Year after year of heavy rain on a sandy soil carries nutrients down past the level any root will ever reach. What is that called?
opts: Leaching
Compaction
Erosion
Oxidation
exp: Leaching is loss downward rather than sideways, and coarse soils suffer it worst because water moves through them so freely. It is one reason a sandy vineyard in a wet region needs feeding while a clay one rarely does, since clay grips nutrients and sand does not.

q: A tractor takes the same wheel track down a row several hundred times a year, and a dense pan builds up under it. What does that do to the vine?
opts: Roots are driven deeper to escape it, which generally improves the wine
It raises the vine's vigour, since a firm bed gives the roots something to anchor against
Very little, since a vine's roots grow only in the top few centimetres
Roots cannot get through the pan, and water sits on it instead of draining away
exp: Compaction squeezes the air out of a soil, and roots need that air as much as they need water. It is worst on wet clay and on the headlands where machinery turns, and undoing it means ripping the ground open, which is far more disruptive than avoiding it in the first place.

q: Decayed plant and animal material worked into a soil binds the fine particles into crumbs and holds several times its own weight in water. What is that fraction called?
opts: Humus, the organic matter of the soil
The clay fraction
The parent rock
Active lime
exp: Organic matter is what turns dust into structure: it glues particles into crumbs so the soil can hold air and water at once rather than one or the other. It also feeds the fungi and bacteria that make nutrients available, and it is the part of a soil a grower can genuinely rebuild.

q: A hillside is cut into level steps before a single vine goes into it. Beyond making the ground workable, what does the terrace achieve?
opts: It raises the temperature of the whole slope by several degrees
It removes the need to graft the vines onto any rootstock
It allows the vines to be planted very much closer together
It stops water running straight down the slope, so the soil stays where it is
exp: Water gathers speed down an uninterrupted slope and takes the soil with it, and a level step breaks that run before it can start. The cost is the building and the upkeep: the old stone-walled terraces are made and repaired by hand, and even the modern earth terraces cut by machine so that a tractor can work them leave a hillside among the most expensive ground in a region to farm.
